voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: You've probably seen it in the news: some big AI model has over a hundred billion parameters.
So what actually is a parameter? And what does it mean to have that many?
Last time, we saw that today's AI mostly figures out patterns on its own, from examples. What it ends up with is called a model.
So this time, let's crack a model open and see what's really inside.
A model is basically a machine: you feed an input in one end, and an answer comes out the other.
And on this machine, there's a row of knobs. Turn them to different positions, and the same input gives a different answer.
Those knobs are the parameters.
Here's an example: guessing a taxi fare. We put in the distance in kilometers, and out comes a guess at the price.
At its simplest, this machine needs just two knobs: one for the base fare, and one for the price per kilometer.
To make a guess, it multiplies the per-kilometer price by the distance, then adds the base fare.
Say the base fare is set to ten dollars and the per-kilometer knob to two dollars. For a five-kilometer ride, it guesses twenty dollars.
People decide how the machine does its math. But where each knob is set? Nobody types that in. The machine learns it from examples.
That's all "learning" is: turning the knobs to the right positions.
Here are twelve made-up taxi rides.
Each dot is one ride: the further right, the longer the trip, and the higher up, the more it cost.
Put its guesses on a graph, and the straight line gives you a fare for any distance.
The little vertical line from each dot to that line shows how far off the guess was for that ride.
Let's start with the knobs set pretty much at random: zero base fare, a dollar per kilometer. The line's way too low, and every ride gets underestimated.
Turn the base fare up to ten dollars, and the whole line lifts up.
Now the short rides are pretty close, but the longer the ride, the further off it gets.
So turn the per-kilometer knob, and the line gets steeper. At three fifty a kilometer, we've gone too far: now the long rides are overestimated.
Back the per-kilometer knob off to about two fifty, and nudge the base fare up to ten dollars twenty.
Now the line runs right along the dots, and all those little vertical lines are short.
Once it's tuned, you can actually use it. So ask it: what would a ride of eight kilometers cost?
None of our twelve rides was eight kilometers, but it can still make a guess: about thirty dollars fifty.
So what did this machine actually learn?
Everything it learned from those twelve rides comes down to where those two knobs are set.
The machine itself hasn't changed one bit. Only the knob settings have.
Copy those two numbers onto a scrap of paper, hand it to a friend, and they've got the exact same model.
When people talk about "training a model," all they're really doing is turning knobs.
Two knobs are plenty for guessing a taxi fare. But if you want a model to write essays or chat with people, you need way, way more.
In twenty twenty, OpenAI released G P T three, which has a hundred and seventy-five billion parameters.
That's a hundred and seventy-five billion knobs.
How many is that? Read out one knob setting every second, no eating, no sleeping, and it'd take you over five and a half thousand years.
Obviously, nobody turned all those knobs by hand. Their settings came from training on huge amounts of text.
But it's the same idea as the taxi fare: people pick the math, and the settings are learned.
And a trained model, saved to a file, is mostly just this long, long list of knob settings.
So when the news says "over a hundred billion parameters," it means the machine has over a hundred billion knobs.
In short, a model is a machine with knobs.
And learning just means turning the knobs to the right positions.
But what does "the right positions" actually mean?
Remember those little vertical lines, some long, some short? They're the clue.
That's next time, when we talk about loss functions.
